lead: Two qubits can be so strongly correlated that neither has a definite state of its own. The joint state is entangled: it cannot be written as one state for qubit A times one state for qubit B. Bell states are the four standard examples. They power quantum key distribution, teleportation and Bell tests. This chapter defines entanglement by non-factorability, lists the Bell states, and explains the EPR argument and why entanglement cannot send a signal.
prereq: You need: tensor products and reduced states from Chapter 2.6, and measurement from Chapter 2.5.

blocks.text: A product state of two qubits is |ψ⟩ = |α⟩<sub>A</sub> ⊗ |β⟩<sub>B</sub>. Write |α⟩ = a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ and |β⟩ = c|0⟩ + d|1⟩. The amplitudes a, b, c, d are complex numbers. For each qubit, |a|²+|b|²=1 and |c|²+|d|²=1. A joint state is entangled when no such product can reproduce it.

blocks.where: a, b, c, d are complex amplitudes; |a|²+|b|²=1 and |c|²+|d|²=1.

blocks.text: Non-factorability is the definition. The whole has definite joint properties, but neither part has a pure state of its own. For the Bell states below the reduced state is I/2, the maximally mixed state, and that is why Alice's local measurement looks perfectly random. A general entangled state gives a reduced state that is mixed but not necessarily I/2; only maximally entangled states give I/2.

items: Write the target state in the basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩.
Expand the product (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩) and collect the four coefficients.
Match the four coefficients to the target.
Solve the four equations. A contradiction means the state is entangled.

blocks.text: Use this test on |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2. Matching gives ac=1/√2, ad=0, bc=0, bd=1/√2. The next section solves it fully.

The four Bell states are an orthonormal basis for two qubits. Each has two nonzero amplitudes of magnitude 1/√2. The square of each nonzero amplitude is 1/2. A minus sign is a relative phase; it changes interference, not the measurement probabilities in the Z basis.

“Same bits” means 00 or 11. “Different bits” means 01 or 10. Normalisation holds because each state has Σ|amplitude|² = 1. Orthogonality holds because the inner product of any two different Bell states is 0. Measuring one qubit in Z gives 0 or 1 with probability 1/2, always. The other qubit's result is fixed by the first result and by which Bell state the pair is in.

Alice's marginal is I/2 no matter what Bob does locally. Bob cannot change Alice's outcome statistics by choosing a gate or a measurement on his qubit. Entanglement gives correlation, not communication. An unknown quantum state cannot be copied, and this includes a qubit that is part of an entangled pair; see the No-cloning theorem chapter.

The EPR argument uses an entangled pair. Alice measures her qubit and instantly knows what Bob would get for the same measurement. EPR assumed local realism: no influence travels faster than light, and physical properties exist before measurement. Then Bob's bit must have been fixed all along. Quantum mechanics says Bob's bit is not fixed until measured. EPR concluded that quantum mechanics is incomplete.

Quantum mechanics escapes because the local outcomes are random. The correlation appears only when Alice and Bob compare classical records. Choosing a measurement on one side does not change the other side's marginal. This is no-signalling. A Bell test turns the disagreement into an experiment; local hidden variables obey CHSH ≤ 2, while quantum mechanics reaches 2√2, as Chapter 2.8 shows. Some syllabi call this topic “Bell states” and the “EPR paradox”.

figure.caption: Following the worked example: matching coefficients forces ad = bc = 0, and a = 0 or d = 0 makes ac or bd zero, so |Φ+⟩ cannot be written as a product. A Z measurement then gives only 00 or 11, each with probability 1/2, so Bob's bit always equals Alice's.

spec.title: Is |Φ+⟩ entangled?
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow for |Φ+⟩: matching the four coefficients gives ac = bd = 1/√2 and ad = bc = 0, but ad = 0 forces a = 0 or d = 0 and each choice makes ac or bd zero, so no product form exists; measuring in Z then gives only 00 or 11, each with probability 1/2, so Bob's bit equals Alice's.

examples.question: Show that |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 is entangled. Try to write it as (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩). Then Alice measures her qubit in the computational basis. Give the joint probabilities and Bob's state after each Alice outcome.
steps: Expand the product: (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩) = ac|00⟩ + ad|01⟩ + bc|10⟩ + bd|11⟩.
Match coefficients with |Φ+⟩: ac = 1/√2, ad = 0, bc = 0, bd = 1/√2.
From ad = 0, either a = 0 or d = 0. If a = 0 then ac = 0, contradicting ac = 1/√2. If d = 0 then bd = 0, contradicting bd = 1/√2. So ad = 0 is impossible.
The same contradiction follows from bc = 0. No complex numbers a, b, c, d satisfy all four equations, so |Φ+⟩ is entangled.
Write the state as (1/√2)|0⟩<sub>A</sub>|0⟩<sub>B</sub> + (1/√2)|1⟩<sub>A</sub>|1⟩<sub>B</sub>. By the Born rule, p(00) = |1/√2|² = 1/2 and p(11) = |1/√2|² = 1/2. Also p(01) = 0 and p(10) = 0.
If Alice gets 0, the state collapses to |0⟩<sub>A</sub>|0⟩<sub>B</sub>, so Bob has |0⟩. If Alice gets 1, Bob has |1⟩. Each Alice outcome has probability 1/2.
examples.answer: The amplitudes must satisfy ac=bd=1/√2≈0.7071 and ad=bc=0, which is impossible, so |Φ+⟩ is entangled; p(00)=p(11)=0.5 and Bob's state is |0⟩ or |1⟩ matching Alice's bit.

traps: Thinking entanglement sends a signal. Local outcomes are random; the correlation shows only after Alice and Bob compare classical records.
Forgetting the normalisation 1/√2 in a Bell state. Each nonzero amplitude has magnitude 1/√2, so each outcome pair has probability 1/2.
Calling any correlated pair entangled. Classical correlation can exist without entanglement; the test is non-factorability of the joint state.
Confusing the Bell states with the basis states |00⟩ and |11⟩. A Bell state is a superposition, not a single computational-basis state.
Saying measurement on Alice changes Bob's state faster than light. The update is a bookkeeping rule for the joint state, not a physical message.

quiz.q: Define an entangled state of two qubits.
quiz.a: A joint state is entangled if it cannot be written as a product |ψ⟩<sub>A</sub> ⊗ |φ⟩<sub>B</sub> of two single-qubit states.

quiz.q: Write the four Bell states with their normalisation.
Why is |Φ+⟩ not a product state? Use the coefficient equations.
quiz.a: Expanding (a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩) forces ac=1/√2, ad=0, bc=0, bd=1/√2. ad=0 needs a=0 or d=0, and each choice contradicts another equation. No product form exists.

quiz.q: For |Ψ−⟩=(|01⟩−|10⟩)/√2, Alice measures her qubit in Z and gets 0. What is Bob's state and what was the probability of Alice's outcome?
quiz.a: The probability is 1/2. The state collapses to |0⟩<sub>A</sub>|1⟩<sub>B</sub>, so Bob has |1⟩.

quiz.q: For |Φ+⟩, what are p(00) and p(01) when both qubits are measured in Z?
Explain why entanglement does not allow faster-than-light communication.
quiz.a: Alice's local outcome is random with probability 1/2, and Bob's reduced state is I/2 regardless of Alice's measurement. A message needs a controllable change in Bob's statistics; entanglement gives none. Only comparing records later reveals the correlation.

quiz.q: State the EPR argument and say what a Bell test adds.
quiz.a: EPR: perfect correlations plus local realism imply pre-existing values, so quantum mechanics is incomplete. A Bell test: local hidden variables obey CHSH ≤ 2, while quantum mechanics gives 2√2; experiments favour quantum mechanics.

beyond: Not for the exam. Entanglement is the resource behind quantum key distribution (E91), teleportation, superdense coding and quantum networks. Hardware groups distribute entangled photons over fibre and free space. Bell tests have been closed for locality and detection loopholes in several experiments. Search next for “Bell state”, “CHSH inequality”, “no-signalling” and “entanglement swapping”.
